name: Part definition
description: A class of physical or logical system components that has identity and structure and can own parts, ports and behaviour. Use it for anything you would draw as a block.
difference: An item can be a thing that flows or is carried (material, energy, data) but is not a structural component of the system; a part is the thing that is assembled and decomposed.

name: Part usage
description: A particular use of a part definition inside an owning context: this assembly contains one of these, in this role.
from: a definition body that allows this kind
to: part definitions (`:`), or other part usages it subsets (`:>`)
difference: A part usage is a structural member of its owner (the controller inside the charger). An item usage is something that moves or is handled and is not decomposed as part of the system.

name: Attribute definition
description: A definition of a data type: a value with no identity (a number with unit, a record of fields, a quantity kind).
difference: An enumeration is a closed list of named values. An attribute definition is an open data type.

name: Attribute usage
description: A named value held by a definition or usage, typed by an attribute definition (for example `ratedPower : PowerValue`).
from: a definition body that allows this kind
to: attribute definitions (`:`), or other attribute usages it subsets (`:>`)
difference: An attribute usage is a value owned by its parent. A reference usage only points at something owned elsewhere.

name: Item definition
description: A class of things that can flow, be stored, or be handled: material, energy, data, a document, a person as a payload. Not a structural component.
difference: A part definition is a structural component with ports and parts. An item definition is what moves between or through parts.

name: Item usage
description: One use of an item definition: a payload on a flow, or something a part carries or stores.
from: a definition body that allows this kind
to: item definitions (`:`), or other item usages it subsets (`:>`)
difference: An item usage is typically the payload of a flow or something held; a part usage is a component in the decomposition.

name: Port definition
description: A definition of an interaction point on a part: what can enter or leave through it (directed features, nested ports).
difference: An interface definition describes a connection between two ports. A port definition describes one end.

name: Port usage
description: A named interaction point on a part, typed by a port definition. A `~` before the type makes it the conjugate (inputs and outputs reversed).
from: a definition body that allows this kind
to: port definitions (`:`), or other port usages it subsets (`:>`)
difference: A port is a boundary of its owner; a part is a component inside it.

name: Connection definition
description: A definition of a relationship between parts that has its own properties or structure, with two or more ends.
difference: An interface definition constrains connections between ports. A connection definition is a link between any features, with no port requirement.

name: Connection (connect)
description: A particular link between the features of a context, optionally typed by a connection definition (`connect a to b`).
difference: An interface usage connects ports. A connection usage connects any features.

name: Interface definition
description: A definition of a connection between ports that fixes what passes across it (the ends are port definitions).
difference: An interface definition ends on ports and is about what crosses a boundary. A connection definition ends on any feature.

name: Interface usage
keyword: interface : Def connect a to b;
description: A use of an interface definition connecting two ports: `interface : PowerInterface connect charger.out to vehicle.in;`
difference: An interface usage is a connection restricted to ports and typed by an interface definition.
example: interface : PowerInterface connect charger.out to vehicle.in;

name: Allocation definition
description: A definition of an allocation relationship between a source and a target, for example logical to physical, or function to component.
difference: Satisfy says a design element meets a requirement. Allocate maps any element (function, requirement, part) onto another and carries no obligation to prove it.

name: Allocation (allocate)
description: A statement that one element is allocated to another (`allocate a to b;`). Allocation says where something is done or realised; it does not say how.
from: any definition or usage (source): a requirement, function, part
difference: Allocate maps any element onto any other and asserts nothing about meeting a need. Satisfy relates a design element to a requirement and says the need is met.

name: Flow definition
description: A definition of an item flow: what is transferred between two features (a payload type and ends).
difference: A flow definition is about something moving. A connection definition is a link with no direction of travel.

name: Flow
keyword: flow of P from a to b;
description: A transfer of a payload from one feature to another (`flow of Current from a.out to b.in;`).
from: a feature that outputs the payload
to: a feature that inputs the payload
difference: A flow transfers a payload and implies no order. A succession flow also fixes that the source finishes first.
example: flow of Current from a.out to b.in;

name: Occurrence definition
description: A definition of anything that exists over time and can have a start and end. Part, item and action definitions are all kinds of occurrence.
difference: A part definition is an occurrence that is also a structural component. A plain occurrence has time extent only.

name: Occurrence usage
description: A use of an occurrence definition. Prefix forms (`individual`, `snapshot`, `timeslice`) say which slice or particular it is.
from: a definition body that allows this kind
to: occurrence definitions (`:`), or other occurrence usages it subsets (`:>`)
difference: Use the specific usage (part, item, action) when one fits; a plain occurrence is the generic parent.

name: Individual definition
description: A definition of a single, particular thing (this serial number, this vehicle) rather than a class.
difference: A part definition is a class of things. An individual definition is one particular thing.

name: Individual usage
description: A usage that refers to one individual over its life; combine with `snapshot` and `timeslice` for states in time.
from: a definition body that allows this kind
to: individual definitions (`:`), or other individual usages it subsets (`:>`)
difference: Use an individual only when one concrete thing matters (a test article); otherwise model the class.

name: Action definition
description: A definition of behaviour: something that happens, with inputs, outputs and a decomposition into steps.
difference: A state definition describes what a thing is in over time, with entry, do and exit. An action definition is what happens, step by step.

name: Action usage
description: A step of behaviour inside another action or a part (`action charge : ChargeVehicle;`).
from: a definition body that allows this kind
to: action definitions (`:`), or other action usages it subsets (`:>`)
difference: An action usage is a step owned by its parent. A perform usage says that a part performs an action defined elsewhere.

name: State definition
description: A definition of a condition a thing can be in, with entry, do and exit behaviour and transitions to other states.
difference: An action definition describes behaviour that finishes. A state definition describes a condition that persists until a transition leaves it.

name: State usage
description: A state of its owner, possibly with nested states (`state ready;`).
from: a definition body that allows this kind
to: state definitions (`:`), or other state usages it subsets (`:>`)
difference: A state usage belongs to its owner. An exhibit usage says a part exhibits a state machine defined elsewhere.

name: Constraint definition
description: A definition of a Boolean condition over features: it holds or does not (`voltage <= 480 [V]`).
difference: A calculation definition returns a value. A constraint definition returns true or false.
example: constraint def MaxVoltage { in v; v <= 480 [V] }

name: Constraint usage
description: A use of a constraint definition, or an inline condition, inside a definition or requirement.
from: a definition body that allows this kind
to: constraint definitions (`:`), or other constraint usages it subsets (`:>`)
difference: A constraint usage states a condition. An assert constraint usage asserts it must hold (or not, with `not`).

name: Requirement definition
description: A definition of a stated need: a subject, a text and constraints that a design must meet.
difference: A requirement definition is a constraint with a subject, an id and a text that stakeholders own. A constraint definition is a pure condition with no stakeholder.

name: Requirement usage
description: A use of a requirement definition at a place in a requirement tree or inside a verification objective.
from: a definition body that allows this kind
to: requirement definitions (`:`), or other requirement usages it subsets (`:>`)
difference: A requirement usage is the requirement itself in a tree. A satisfy relationship says a design element meets it.

name: Concern definition
description: A definition of a stakeholder interest that views and requirements address (cost, safety, serviceability).
difference: A requirement states what must hold. A concern states what someone cares about, before it is turned into requirements.

name: Concern usage
description: A use of a concern, framed by a viewpoint or requirement (`frame concern`).
from: a definition body that allows this kind
to: concern definitions (`:`), or other concern usages it subsets (`:>`)
difference: A concern usage is a standalone interest. A framed concern usage is a concern placed inside a viewpoint or requirement via `frame`.

name: Calculation definition
description: A definition of a computation that takes inputs and returns a value (a function in the mathematical sense).
difference: A constraint definition yields true or false. A calculation definition yields any value.
example: calc def Power { in v; in i; return v*i; }

name: Calculation usage
description: A use of a calculation to derive a value inside a definition.
from: a definition body that allows this kind
to: calculation definitions (`:`), or other calculation usages it subsets (`:>`)
difference: An attribute usage holds a value. A calculation usage computes it from inputs.

name: Case definition
description: A generic definition of an analysis, verification or use case that has a subject, objective and result. The specific kinds below are normally used instead.
difference: A use case definition is a case about actors and a subject using a system. A plain case is the generic parent.

name: Case usage
description: A use of a generic case definition in a context, with its subject and objective. Prefer the specific usage kinds.
from: a definition body that allows this kind
to: case definitions (`:`), or other case usages it subsets (`:>`)
difference: Prefer use case, analysis or verification; use plain case only for something that fits none.

name: Analysis case definition
description: A definition of an analysis that computes results about a subject for an objective (trade study, thermal analysis).
difference: A verification case checks a requirement against a subject and produces a verdict. An analysis case computes values and need not judge anything.

name: Analysis case usage
description: A use of an analysis case with its subject and result.
from: a definition body that allows this kind
to: analysis case definitions (`:`), or other analysis case usages it subsets (`:>`)
difference: An analysis usage computes. A verification usage decides pass or fail against requirements.

name: Verification case definition
description: A definition of how requirements are verified: a subject, a method and an objective that verifies requirements and returns a verdict.
difference: A verification case ends in a verdict on requirements. An analysis case ends in a computed result.

name: Verification case usage
description: A use of a verification case applied to a subject (`verification v : TestCharger;`).
from: a definition body that allows this kind
to: verification case definitions (`:`), or other verification case usages it subsets (`:>`)
difference: A verification usage is the planned test or inspection. A verify usage inside its objective names the requirement it checks.

name: Use case definition
description: A definition of how actors use a subject to get a result, with included and extended behaviour.
difference: An action definition is behaviour. A use case definition is the goal of actors using a subject, which then refers to actions.

name: Use case usage
description: A use of a use case, in the subject's context (`use case charge : ChargeVehicleUseCase;`).
from: a definition body that allows this kind
to: use case definitions (`:`), or other use case usages it subsets (`:>`)
difference: A use case usage is a goal. An include usage embeds another use case inside it.

name: View definition
description: A definition of a rendered selection of model content that answers a viewpoint.
difference: A viewpoint definition says what view is needed and for whom. A view definition is the thing that shows it.

name: View usage
description: A use of a view that exposes elements and renders them (`view v { expose Charger::*; render asTreeDiagram; }`).
from: a definition body that allows this kind
to: view definitions (`:`), or other view usages it subsets (`:>`)
difference: A view usage selects and renders content. A viewpoint usage states the stakeholder need that the view answers.

name: Viewpoint definition
description: A definition of the stakeholder concerns a view has to address.
difference: A viewpoint holds concerns. A view holds the content.

name: Viewpoint usage
description: A use of a viewpoint that a view conforms to.
from: a definition body that allows this kind
to: viewpoint definitions (`:`), or other viewpoint usages it subsets (`:>`)
difference: A viewpoint holds the concerns; a view holds the content that answers them.

name: Rendering definition
description: A definition of how a view's content is presented (tree, table, diagram).
difference: A view selects content. A rendering decides how it looks.

name: Rendering usage
description: A use of a rendering inside a view (`render asTable;`).
from: a definition body that allows this kind
to: rendering definitions (`:`), or other rendering usages it subsets (`:>`)
difference: A view selects content; a rendering decides how that content looks.

name: Metadata definition
description: A definition of an annotation type attached to elements (a tag with typed fields such as `Safety`, `Approved`).
difference: An attribute definition describes data inside the model. A metadata definition describes data about model elements and can be applied to them.
example: metadata def Safety { attribute level : Integer; }

name: Metadata usage
description: A use that attaches metadata to an element: `@Safety { level = 3; }` or `#Safety part x;`.
from: a definition body that allows this kind
to: metadata definitions (`:`), or other metadata usages it subsets (`:>`)
difference: Metadata annotates another element; an attribute is a value of its own element.

name: Enumeration definition
description: A definition of a closed set of named values.
difference: An attribute definition allows any value of its type. An enumeration allows only its named values.
example: enum def Mode { enum on; enum off; }

name: Enumeration usage
description: A use of an enumeration definition: a feature whose value is one of the named values.
from: a definition body that allows this kind
to: enumeration definitions (`:`), or other enumeration usages it subsets (`:>`)
difference: An attribute usage may hold any value of its type; an enumeration usage holds one of the named values only.

name: Specialization (definition)
description: The relationship that makes one definition a more specific kind of another. The specializing definition inherits every feature of the general one and may add or narrow features.
to: a definition of the same kind (a part def specializes a part def)
difference: Specialization relates two definitions (kind of). Typing relates a usage to its definition (instance of). A part def `Charger :> MHECharger` is a kind of MHE charger; a part `c : Charger` is one charger.

name: Feature typing
description: The relationship that says a usage is an instance of a definition (`part c : Charger`). The usage gets the definition's features.
to: one or more definitions of a compatible kind
difference: Typing is usage to definition (this is one of those). Specialization is definition to definition (this is a kind of that).

name: Subsetting
description: The relationship that says the things a usage identifies are a subset of the things another usage identifies (`part leftWheel :> wheels`). The subsetting usage inherits the other's type and multiplicity bounds.
to: another usage of a compatible kind, in an ancestor definition
difference: Subsetting adds a narrower usage next to the original, which still exists. Redefinition replaces the original inside this context.

name: Redefinition
description: The relationship that replaces an inherited usage in a specializing definition with a refined one (`:>>` or `redefines`). Use it to narrow a type, fix a value or change a multiplicity in a specialization.
to: an inherited usage of a compatible kind
difference: Redefinition replaces; the original is no longer a separate member of the specialization. Subsetting keeps the original and adds a subset of it.
from: a usage in a specializing definition

name: Reference subsetting
description: The relationship that makes a usage refer to another feature rather than own a new one (`::>` or `references`). The usage is a reference to something owned elsewhere.
to: a feature owned elsewhere in the model
difference: Subsetting makes a new member that is a subset. Reference subsetting makes the usage point at an existing feature and own nothing.

name: Cross subsetting
description: The relationship that says what a connection end sees from the far end of the connection (`crosses`). It defines the navigation across an association.
to: a feature reachable from the other end
difference: Cross subsetting is about navigation across a connection end. Reference subsetting is a plain reference.

name: Conjugation
description: The relationship that makes a port definition the mirror of another: inputs become outputs and outputs become inputs (`~` before the type). It saves writing a second definition for the other end of an interface.
difference: Typing gives the usage the definition's features as written. Conjugation gives them reversed in direction.
from: a port usage, or a conjugated port definition

name: Dependency
description: A directed relationship stating that the client depends on the supplier, with no further semantics. Use it when no more specific relationship fits, and name the reason in a comment.
difference: A dependency has no semantic and no structure. An allocation says one element is realised by another and is a typed mapping.

name: Import (membership)
description: Makes a member of another namespace visible by its simple name in this one. The imported element stays owned by its original namespace.
difference: An import makes an element visible without a new name. An alias gives it a second name.

name: Import (namespace)
description: Makes every public member of another namespace visible. `::*` brings the direct members, `::**` brings the members of nested namespaces as well.
difference: A namespace import brings in everything; a membership import brings in one named member.

name: Alias
description: Gives an existing element another name in a namespace. The element is not copied or owned by the alias.
difference: An alias adds a second name; an import adds visibility under the existing name.

name: Filter
description: A Boolean condition on a package that limits which of its members an import or view sees (`filter @Safety;`).
to: a Boolean expression, often a metadata test
difference: A filter limits what is seen; expose names what a view shows.

name: Package
description: The basic container that groups elements and gives them qualified names. Every model element lives in a package. In MDSE a package is also a note's `package` wrapper and a folder.
to: its members: definitions, usages, imports, annotations
difference: A package is for your model content. A library package marks reusable library content and is excluded from some checks.

name: Library package
description: A package marked as reusable library content, such as units, quantities or a company part catalog.
difference: Same structure as a package; the `library` marker tells tools it is shared, not project content.
example: library package Parts { part def Bolt; }

name: Comment
description: Free text attached to an element or to the enclosing namespace. Unlike `//` or `/* */` that tools drop, a `comment` is a model element that is kept.
difference: A comment is a note about elements and may be anywhere. Documentation (`doc`) is the description of its owner.
example: comment about Charger /* Rated for 480 VAC */

name: Documentation
description: The description of the element that owns it. Requirements keep their text here.
difference: Documentation describes its owner and has no `about`; a comment may annotate others.
example: part def Charger { doc /* A 30 kW DC charger. */ }

name: Textual representation
description: Embeds code in another language (a formula, a script) as the body of a model element.
difference: Documentation is human text; a textual representation is executable or parseable in the named language.

name: Prefix metadata
description: Applies a metadata definition to an element with `#` in front of its declaration.
difference: A prefix is shorthand for the same annotation written as `@Tag` in the body.

name: Metadata annotation
description: Attaches a metadata value to an element in its body (`@Safety { level = 3; }`) or to others with `about`.
difference: Same meaning as `#Tag`; the body form can set fields.

name: Visibility
description: Controls whether a member is visible from outside its namespace.
difference: Visibility limits what can be seen; an import chooses what to bring in.

name: Feature modifiers
keyword: abstract | variation | ref | readonly | derived | end | constant | ordered | nonunique
description: Prefix and suffix words that change how a definition or usage behaves: `abstract` (cannot be instantiated), `variation` (choose one variant), `ref` (reference only), `derived`, `ordered`, `nonunique`, `end` (a connection end).
difference: Modifiers change kind and behaviour. Multiplicity changes how many.

name: Multiplicity
description: How many of a usage may exist: `[3]`, `[0..1]`, `[1..*]`. This is how quantities live in the model.
difference: Multiplicity changes how many; modifiers change what kind.

name: Value binding
description: Gives a usage a value or a default value (`ratedPower = 30 [kW]`). `:=` is an initial value, `default =` can be overridden.
difference: A value binds the usage's value; redefinition changes the usage itself.

name: Variation and variant
keyword: variation part def V { variant part a; }
description: Declares a variation point whose members are the allowed choices (variants). A configuration picks one.
difference: Variants live inside one variation point and are chosen per configuration; specialization creates a permanent subtype.
example: variation part def Cable { variant part short : ShortCable; variant part long : LongCable; }

name: Reference usage
description: A usage that points at something owned elsewhere, such as a parameter, a subject or an end. It owns nothing.
difference: A reference does not own its value; an attribute usage owns it.

name: Parameter direction
keyword: in x; out y; inout z
description: The direction keywords on a usage declare whether it is an input, an output or both of its owner (`in`, `out`, `inout`). They apply to action, calc, constraint and port members.
difference: `in`/`out` declare typed parameters; `return` declares the single result of a calc.
example: action a { in x : Real; out y : Real; }
from: a usage in an action, calc, constraint, case or port

name: Return
description: Declares the result of a calculation or expression-bearing definition.
difference: `return` names the one result; `out` can be any number of outputs.
example: calc def Double { in x : Real; return : Real = x*2; }

name: Event occurrence
description: Marks an occurrence that happens at a point in time within a context, such as a message being received. It can reference an existing occurrence.
difference: An event is a moment; a snapshot is the state of a thing at a moment.
from: an occurrence, part, state or action body

name: Snapshot
description: A part or occurrence frozen at one moment in time.
difference: A snapshot has no duration; a timeslice does.

name: Timeslice
description: A part or occurrence over a span of its life, such as the time a charger is in service.
difference: A timeslice has duration; a snapshot is one instant.

name: Actor
description: A part that interacts with the subject of a case or requirement: the driver, the service engineer, an external system.
difference: An actor takes part in the interaction. A stakeholder has an interest in the outcome and may never interact.
from: a use case, requirement, verification or analysis body

name: Stakeholder
description: A party with an interest in a requirement or viewpoint.
difference: A stakeholder cares about the outcome; an actor performs in the scenario.

name: Subject
description: The thing a requirement, case or analysis is about. In a requirement the subject is what must satisfy it.
difference: The subject is a special reference with a role; a plain reference has none.
example: requirement def R { subject c : Charger; }
from: a requirement, case or view body

name: Objective
description: The goal of a case: the requirement(s) a verification must show, or what an analysis must answer.
difference: An objective is the requirement owned by a case; a requirement usage stands on its own in a tree.
example: verification def V { objective { verify r; } }
from: a case, analysis or verification body

name: Assert constraint
description: States that a constraint holds (or, with `not`, does not hold) within the owner.
difference: A plain constraint usage names a condition. An assertion makes the owner claim it.

name: Assume and require constraint
keyword: assume constraint c { } / require constraint c { }
description: The parts of a requirement: `assume` is what must hold for the requirement to apply, `require` is what the subject must meet.
difference: They live inside a requirement and have a role; a free constraint usage has none.
example: requirement def R { require constraint { v <= 480 } }

name: Frame
description: Names a concern that a requirement or viewpoint addresses.
difference: `frame` puts the concern into the requirement or viewpoint; a concern usage on its own is a standalone interest.
example: viewpoint def V { frame concern safety : Safety; }

name: Expose
description: Names the model content a view shows.
difference: Expose selects what a view displays; a filter narrows an import or package.

name: Render
description: Selects how a view is displayed.
difference: `render` is the statement inside a view; a rendering usage is the thing named.

name: Perform
description: States that a part performs an action: the link from structure to behaviour. The action may be declared there or referenced.
to: an action definition or action usage
difference: `perform` binds an action to the part that does it. An action usage on its own is just a step with no performer.
from: a part definition or part usage (the performer)

name: Exhibit
description: States that a part exhibits a state machine: the link from structure to states.
difference: `exhibit` ties a state machine to the part that shows it; a state usage alone belongs to a state or action context.
from: a part definition or usage (the exhibitor)

name: Include
description: States that one use case always runs another as part of itself.
difference: An include is mandatory reuse inside a use case. A plain use case usage `[0..1]` is optional (the MDSE extend form).

name: Satisfy
description: States that a design element (a part, action or state) satisfies a requirement. It does not prove it; verification does.
difference: Satisfy says the design meets the requirement. Verify says a test or analysis shows it does.
from: a part, action, state or other definition or usage (the satisfier)

name: Verify
description: Inside a verification objective, names a requirement the case verifies.
difference: Verify belongs to a verification case and records how a requirement is checked. Satisfy belongs to the design and says it is met.
example: verification def V { objective { verify RemoteControl; } }

name: Binding connector
description: States that two features always have the same value or identify the same thing.
to: a feature of a compatible type
difference: Binding says two features are equal. A connection says they are linked and may be distinct.

name: Succession
description: States that one occurrence (action, state, event) ends before another starts.
to: an action, state or other occurrence usage
difference: A succession orders two occurrences with no trigger or guard. A transition moves between states and can carry a trigger, guard and effect.
from: an action, state or other occurrence usage

name: Transition
keyword: transition first a accept sig if g do act then b;
description: A move from one state (or action) to the next, with an optional trigger (`accept`), guard (`if`) and effect (`do`).
difference: A transition has a trigger, guard and effect and applies between states. A succession only orders.
example: transition first idle accept start then charging;

name: Succession flow
keyword: succession flow of P from a to b;
description: A flow whose source must finish before the target starts.
difference: A succession flow adds ordering. A flow only transfers.
example: succession flow of Current from a.out to b.in;

name: Message
keyword: message m of P from a to b;
description: A transfer of a payload shown between occurrences without saying which features carry it. Used in interaction (sequence) descriptions.
difference: A message is described between events in time. A flow is between features.
example: message m of Request from a.send to b.receive;

name: Accept
description: An action that waits to receive a payload (a signal, an item) and then proceeds.
difference: Accept receives; send transmits.

name: Send
description: An action that sends a payload through a port or to a target.
difference: Send transmits; accept receives.
example: action a { send s via out1; }

name: Assign
description: An action that sets the value of a feature.
difference: Assign changes a value at a point in behaviour. A value binding gives the value as a definition.

name: Decide, merge, fork, join
description: Control nodes in an action: `decide` chooses one branch, `merge` rejoins branches, `fork` starts parallel branches, `join` waits for all.
difference: A control node is a point in the flow; a succession is the arrow between points.
example: action a { fork f; join j; }

name: If
description: Runs one block of actions or another depending on a condition.
to: a Boolean expression and action blocks
difference: `if` is structured and inline; `decide` draws the branch as a node with successions.
example: action a { if ok { action x; } }

name: While, loop, for
keyword: while c { } / loop { } until c; / for x in xs { }
description: Repeats a block of actions while a condition holds, until one does, or for each item.
to: a Boolean expression, a collection and an action block
difference: Loops repeat; `if` runs once.
example: action a { while more { action step; } }

name: Terminate
description: Ends the enclosing occurrence early, before its normal end, and everything it contains.
difference: Terminate stops; a control node steers.

name: Entry, do, exit
keyword: entry action a; do action b; exit action c;
description: The actions a state runs when entered, while in it, and when left.
difference: State actions run inside a state. A transition's effect runs while moving between states.
example: state s { entry action init; do action run; exit action stop; }

name: Expression
keyword: a + b;  v <= 480 [V];  x.y.z;  x ? a : b
description: Operators, feature chains and units that compute or compare values. They appear in constraints, calculations, values, guards and requirement conditions.
to: features, literals with units, and other expressions
difference: An expression computes or tests. A value binding attaches the result to a usage.
from: a constraint, calc, value binding, guard or condition
